The Effects of the Wavelength of Light on the Growth of Lettuce (Lactuca sativa) 
Cultivated in Martian Regolith 
 
 
Team Members: Nicolas Smith, Jessica Pierre Toussaint, Jason Mendoza, Suemy 
Valenzuela 
Coach: Davia Hudson-Holness 
 
Team ID: 24577 
Plant the Moon Challenge: Spring 2026

2
Introduction 
To understand the potential of life beyond Earth, there is a strong call for continued space 
exploration. According to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), 
they are returning to the moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, and inspiration 
for a new generation of explorers: the Artemis Generation (NASA, 2024). The scientific 
discoveries from the moon can then be used to gather more information about Mars and 
the solar system. Mars, however, is the ultimate goal for human exploration because it is 
one of the only other places known where life may have existed in the solar system (NASA, 
2023). 
NASA will be exploring Mars and more of the solar system; however, those expeditions 
can be very long and challenging. This means that there will be a need for methods that 
will allow explorers to grow sustainable crops while they complete their mission. 
According to the Plant the Moon Challenge (2024), individuals from various education 
levels are coming together and developing experiments that modify lunar or Martian 
regolith to grow the best nutrient rich crops (2024). The goal of these experiments is to 
maximize the crop yield while limiting the amount of mass that is needed from Earth. 
According to Shaw and Soma (2022), space missions are becoming longer so the quality 
and nutrition of food need to be improved, as the astronauts’ health and wellbeing (both 
physical and mental) are highly dependent on diet (Shaw and Soma, 2022). It is incredibly 
important that the astronauts remain healthy so that they can continue their mission 
providing information that advances scientific discoveries. 
The goal of this project is to investigate how different wavelengths of light impact the 
growth of Butterhead lettuce (Lactua sativa) in Martian regolith. The hypothesis is that the 
growth and physiological development of Butterhead lettuce grown in Martian regolith will 
vary depending on the wavelength of light provided, with plants exposed to combined red 
and blue wavelengths producing greater biomass and chlorophyll content than those grown 
under red, blue, or full-spectrum light alone. 
 
Key terms: Lactuca sativa, Martian regolith simulant, wavelength of light, biomass, 
chlorophyll content

3
Theory 
Martian regolith has been studied for years, and most researchers agree that it does not act 
like Earth soil. Martian regolith is composed of basaltic sand, dust, and crushed volcanic 
rock with almost no organic matter (Let’s Talk Science, 2025). Because it has no 
microorganisms or decomposed plant material, it cannot cycle nutrients the way Earth soil 
does. This also means the regolith has a naturally alkaline pH, usually between 8.5 and 9.5, 
which is far outside the preferred range for crops like lettuce. The alkalinity of Martian 
regolith interferes with the availability of phosphorus, iron, and zinc thus preventing plants 
from absorbing the nutrients they need to survive (Temming, 2020). 
A second major limitation is the presence of perchlorates which are toxic chlorine-based 
salts found across the Martian surface. Perchlorates not only harm plant growth but also 
makes it unsafe for humans if they accumulate in edible leaves (Temming, 2020). Water 
behavior in Martian regolith is also a major challenge. Cartier (2023) reports that regolith 
simulants dry out rapidly and compact into dense layers that restrict root penetration. The 
soil particles are so fine that they either drain water too quickly or trap it in pockets without 
proper aeration. Mathewson (2016) found that lettuce grown in simulants required small, 
frequent waterings to prevent soil hardening and moisture stress. This matches patterns 
seen across multiple Mars-growing studies, which show that soil moisture must be 
controlled carefully to avoid both drought and oversaturation. 
Nutrient deficiencies add another layer of difficulty. Although regolith contains minerals 
such as iron, magnesium, and calcium, it lacks essential macronutrients like nitrogen and 
phosphorus. Because of this, many Earth-based experiments combine Martian simulants 
with soil amendments. Duri et al. (2022) found that mixtures of simulants and organic 
material significantly improved water retention, chlorophyll levels, and overall biomass in 
lettuce. Amendments such as worm castings, compost, manure, and perlite help improve 
soil structure and nutrient availability. 
Since researchers do not have access to Martian soil, they rely on regolith simulants like 
MMS-1which reproduces the chemical and physical properties of Martian basalt, allowing 
controlled experiments on crop growth under Mars like conditions (Kasiviswanathan et al., 
2025). Studies using MMS-1 consistently show that lettuce can grow, but only when the

4
regolith is amended, watered properly, and adjusted chemically to reduce alkalinity. 
Understanding these limitations is important for this project because it explains why the 
regolith must be modified before testing how different wavelengths of light influence 
lettuce growth. 
Scientists and astronauts recognize the constant need for food and nutrition, particularly 
from a sustainable and efficient source. Through trial and error, lettuce (Lactuca sativa) is 
one of the best crop options for many reasons, such as short growth cycle, nutritional value, 
and performance in controlled environments. In a 2019 study by El-Nakhel et al., where 
two varieties of lettuce were compared in terms of performance, both grew quickly, where 
one even managed to outgrow the other, implying a shorter harvest schedule to attain the 
target weight and maturity stage requirement. This fast growth emphasized the efficient 
harvest that can come from lettuce, and even leading to less consumption of water and 
minerals for reaching target produce (El-Nakhel et al., 2019). 
Lettuce’s ability to grow quickly hits one of the goals of an exceptional crop model because 
astronauts’ access to food is always limited. In a 2020 article by Burgess et al., researchers 
presented a theoretical plan to biofortify lettuce crops to increase nutrients that are already 
found in them. In the article, they concluded that lettuce “presents a model starting point 
for the generation of new space farming systems and biofortified crops to meet human 
nutritional requirements” (Burgess et al., 2020). This further strengthens the fact that 
lettuce is a model crop because it offers a meaningful foundation of vitamins, antioxidants, 
and minerals important to an astronaut’s diet. 
Combined with all lettuce’s efficiency, it was also found to be a resilient crop in harsh 
environments. In a 2011 study by Wheeler et al., where many crops were grown in 
controlled environments, the scientists found that lettuce could withstand decompression 
down to ~1.5-2.0 kPa for up to 30 min with no apparent damage. This resilience is also 
clear when it comes to different wavelengths of light. In a 2010 study by Hogewoning et 
al., different wavelengths of light were tested, such as white light, blue light, and red light. 
From this study, it was found that the total biomass under only the red-light spectrums was 
greatly reduced, and that growth and development had been inhibited, which leads to 
decreased chlorophyll content. In the same study, when both red and blue were combined,

5
the physiological disorders associated with leaf development under red light alone were 
eliminated by adding only a small amount of blue light, further supporting the fact that red 
and blue light are needed to promote growth and development of lettuce crops 
(Hogewoning et al., 2010). Different wavelengths of light affect plant growth because 
plants absorb certain parts of the spectrum better than others; photosynthetic pigments 
exhibit maximal absorption in the red and blue regions of the spectrum (Hogewoning et al. 
2010, p. 111). This is why most research focuses on red and blue light emission diodes 
(LEDs) when studying how plants develop in controlled environments. 
Red light, which is usually around 660 nanometers, strongly supports photosynthesis and 
increases plant growth. Hernández and Kubota (2016) found that red wavelengths near 660 
nm significantly enhance biomass accumulation and leaf expansion in leafy vegetables (p. 
45). This wavelength encourages bigger leaves, faster growth, and more total biomass. At 
the same time, too much red light in small or enclosed spaces can create stress. Johkan et 
al. (2012) reported that overexposure to red LEDs increased leaf temperature and caused 
tip burn under enclosed conditions (p. 7), showing that red light must be used with control 
and proper distance. On the other hand, blue light, usually around 450 nanometers, plays a 
different role. It influences chlorophyll formation, the strength of the leaf, and the shape of 
the plant. Stutte (2009) noted that blue light is essential for normal photomorphogenesis 
and chlorophyll development (p. 115). Blue wavelengths increase pigment levels, create 
thicker and darker leaves, and keep plants compact. Pennisi et al. (2019) showed that higher 
amounts of blue light can increase pigments but reduce fresh weight, which confirms that 
red and blue need to be balanced for healthy growth. Full-spectrum light on the other hand, 
provides a wide range of wavelengths similar to natural sunlight. Snowden et al. (2016) 
says that broad-spectrum white LEDs produce morphology similar to sunlight-grown 
plants and serve as an effective control condition in controlled-environment studies (p. 66). 
Full-spectrum lighting creates a natural baseline that helps compare how plants react when 
only red or blue wavelengths are used. 
Research on lettuce and other leafy greens shows the same pattern across different studies. 
A mix of red and blue light produces the strongest and healthiest growth, proving to be the 
best option. Red-dominant conditions increase leaf size, while blue-dominant conditions

6
build stronger leaves with deeper color. Full-spectrum light creates natural-looking plants 
but is less efficient because plants do not use all wavelengths equally as supported by 
NASA’s findings. Hummerick et al. (2020) reported that lettuce grown under red and blue 
LEDs showed robust growth and acceptable morphology for spaceflight crop production 
(p. 4), which matches the results seen in other controlled-environment research. Red light 
increases photosynthesis and leaf expansion, blue light strengthens chlorophyll and 
structure, and full-spectrum light provides a natural point of comparison. These studies 
support the idea that the best approach is a combination of full-spectrum lighting and 
targeted red and blue wavelengths when studying how plants grow in controlled 
environments. 
Overall, lettuce is one of the best crops to cultivate in harsh and nutrient deficient 
conditions, as it can withstand them to a certain extent. In addition, it is full of nutrients 
and is an efficient grower because its rapid growth limits water consumption and the wait 
from seed to harvest. Lettuce has been found to grow best in the combination of blue and 
red light as opposed to being used separately, which supports the project’s hypothesis.

Procedure 
1. Soil Preparation: Each pot was filled with ~100 ml of the soil mixture (50% regolith, 
40% topsoil, 10% perlite and 7.5 grams of worm castings). This will be referred to as 
soil mixture throughout the article. Soil pH and EC were measured on the day of 
planting. 
2. Growth Conditions: Plants were grown indoors under controlled temperature and 
humidity. Light sources were positioned 20–25 cm above the lettuce plants. Plants 
were grown in 3-gallon aquariums that were covered with aluminum foil ensuring 
that plants were only exposed to the appropriate light sources and wavelengths. 
3. Watering Schedule: Each pot received 10 - 15 mL of distilled water depending on the 
moisture level of the plants. Plants were initially watered twice per week, but the 
schedule was modified to once per over the growth period to prevent overwatering of 
the plants. Watering volume and frequency was consistent for all samples. 
4. Monitoring and Measurements: Weekly measurements included plant height, number 
of leaves, number of plants, and chlorophyll content (SPAD – soil and plant analysis 
development). Harvest measurements included fresh and dry weight (after drying at 
60 °C for 48 h), and final soil pH. Room conditions were recorded weekly. 
5. Data Analysis: Data was recorded in an excel spreadsheet and shared using the 
college’s one drive system (Microsoft). Collected data was compared across 
treatments to determine the effect of light wavelength on lettuce growth. Statistical 
analyses such as mean values and standard deviations were calculated to test 
significance.

Discussion & Conclusions 
The growth period spanned seven weeks, as the eighth week coincided with the college’s 
spring break. Throughout this time, plant growth was observed in all soil samples, 
including the 100% Martian regolith, the 100% topsoil, and the soil mixture composed of 
50% Martian regolith, 40% topsoil, 10% perlite, and worm castings as fertilizer. Each soil 
type displayed distinct physical characteristics. The Martian regolith was highly granular, 
allowing water to pass through quickly, while the topsoil was less absorbent, causing water 
to pool on the surface before gradually being absorbed. In contrast, the soil mixture showed 
a balanced combination of drainage and absorption, allowing it to retain moisture more 
effectively. These differences in soil texture presented challenges in maintaining a 
consistent watering schedule, as each sample required varying amounts of water (10 – 15 
mL). As a result, both the watering schedule and volume had to be adjusted throughout the 
growth period. 
 
An additional observation was the presence of condensation within the aquariums exposed 
to the red/blue light combination and the full-spectrum light source, suggesting differences 
in moisture retention under these lighting setups. The average temperature and humidity 
inside the lab were 72 °F and 70%, respectively. However, the temperature and humidity 
within the aquariums varied slightly depending on the light source used. The average 
temperatures in the aquariums exposed to individual red and blue light sources were 76 °F 
and 75 °F, respectively. In comparison, the aquariums with full-spectrum lighting and the 
red/blue light combination had average temperatures of 77 °F and 82 °F, respectively. 
Although the average temperature in the full-spectrum setup appeared similar to that of the 
individual light treatments, the daytime temperatures in this aquarium reached as high as 
80 °F. These elevated temperatures may have contributed to the condensation observed in 
these aquariums; however, this effect was not reflected in the recorded humidity values. A 
likely explanation is that the humidity measurements were taken after harvesting, when the 
plants were no longer present to contribute to moisture levels, potentially resulting in less 
accurate humidity readings.

14
Weekly analysis of soil pH and electrical conductivity indicated that the soil composition, 
rather than the light source, was the primary factor influencing these properties (Figures 1 
and 2). The pH of all soil samples was slightly acidic, ranging from 6.6 to 6.8, which falls 
within the optimal range for most plant growth. Electrical conductivity measurements were 
highest in the 100% topsoil samples, indicating a greater ion concentration compared to 
the 100% Martian regolith and the soil mixture samples. The lettuce seeds successfully 
germinated in all soil types, with visible sprouting occurring within five days of planting. 
However, the growth rates varied across the samples; plants grown in the soil mixture 
exhibited the greatest increase in height, outperforming those grown in both 100% Martian 
regolith and 100% topsoil. These findings suggest that the soil mixture composed of 
Martian regolith, topsoil, perlite, and worm castings provides a more favorable 
environment for plant growth, lessening some of the limitations associated with growth in 
100% Martian regolith. 
 
The superior growth observed in the soil mixture was consistent across all light treatments 
(Figure 3). Within this soil condition, plants grown under red light achieved the greatest 
height, with an average of 10.24 cm over the growth period and a relative growth rate of 
0.28 cm/week. These findings align with previous research indicating that red light can 
enhance plant growth. However, despite their greater height, plants grown under red light 
appeared thin and less robust compared to those grown under the full-spectrum and 
combined red/blue light sources. The plants exposed to full-spectrum and red/blue lighting 
exhibited fuller, healthier morphology, suggesting that while red light promotes elongation, 
a broader light spectrum supports a more balanced plant development. 
 
Chlorophyll content was measured beginning in week four of the growth period, when the 
leaves had reached sufficient size for accurate measurements using a chlorophyll meter. 
Measurements were conducted only on the lettuce plants grown in the soil mixture, as 
leaves from the other soil conditions were too small for reliable measurements. Plants 
grown under the red/blue light combination possessed the highest chlorophyll content, 
followed by those grown under the full-spectrum light source. The average chlorophyll 
content for plants under the red/blue light was 13.44 Soil Plant Analysis Development

15
(SPAD) units, compared to 9.66 SPAD units for plants grown under red light alone (Figure 
4). These results suggest that the combined red/blue light treatment is more effective in 
promoting chlorophyll accumulation than red light alone. 
 
While chlorophyll content is a useful indicator of plant health, biomass provides a more 
direct measure of the effectiveness of the photosynthesis process and therefore the overall 
plant productivity so both fresh and dry biomass were measured at the end of the growth 
period. Fresh biomass was recorded for all plant samples, and the results showed that plants 
grown in the soil mixture produced the highest fresh biomass compared to those grown in 
100% Martian regolith and 100% topsoil (Figure 5). Among the light treatments, plants 
grown under full-spectrum lighting exhibited slightly higher fresh biomass than those 
grown under the red/blue light combination, with average values of 6.94 grams and 6.02 
grams, respectively. 
 
Because fresh biomass includes retained water, dry biomass was also measured to provide 
a more accurate assessment of plant growth. Dry biomass measurements were conducted 
only on the soil mixture samples, as these exhibited the most robust and healthy growth. 
The samples were dried overnight in an oven set to 60 °C prior to measurement. Results 
indicated that plants grown under full-spectrum and combined red/blue light produced 
greater dry biomass than those grown under individual red or blue light treatments. Among 
these, the full-spectrum condition yielded slightly higher dry biomass than the red/blue 
combination, with a minimal difference of 0.08 grams units between the two (Figure 6). 
 
The results obtained are consistent with previous research indicating that while individual 
red and blue light sources can support plant growth, a combination of both is necessary to 
promote strong, healthy development (Figure 7). Although plants grown under single-
wavelength light sources exhibited greater height, those exposed to combined red/blue and 
full-spectrum lighting demonstrated superior overall health. This was shown by higher 
chlorophyll content and greater biomass, supporting the hypothesis that plants exposed to 
combined red and blue wavelengths produce greater biomass and chlorophyll levels than 
those grown under red or blue light alone.

16
These results indicate that the soil mixture, when combined with either red/blue or full-
spectrum lighting, supports the growth of robust and healthy plants. Future research could 
focus on evaluating the nutritional viability and overall quality of these plants. 
Measurements such as photosynthesis efficiency and nutritional composition would 
provide deeper insight into not just plant growth but also their suitability as a nutritious 
food source.
